proposals.name: Payoff density: no word that is not carrying the joke
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the caption is doing comic work versus supplying scaffolding. Delete every word that could be cut without losing the joke; the score is how little is left over. 10 = the caption is essentially punchline only, with setup carried implicitly (a single coined word, a three-word line, a clipped label); nothing can be trimmed. 5 = one clause of ordinary setup feeding one clause of payoff, with a few discardable words. 0 = a long, well-formed conversational sentence in which the comic content is a small terminal fraction and half the words are ordinary chat that could be cut with no loss. Judge on proportion, not absolute length: a long caption whose every clause bends the joke still scores high.
proposals.rationale: The dense-high side is dominated by extreme compression -- R07 ('wreckmaninoff'), R19 ('he got indicted'), R34 ('it's so ewe'), R59 ('this is taking an eternity') are one to four words and rank .794-.996 dense while the scorecard puts them at .038-.452. The dense-low side is systematically padded: R30 ('if you're free after work, i know this hole-in-the-wall place you'll love') and R56 ('i can usually identify a bird by the song, but i think he's doing a cover') are fluent full sentences at card .938/.783 but dense .170/.006. A scorecard that rewards completeness and readable setup-then-payoff structure will invert exactly this axis.

proposals.name: Punch lands on the last word
proposals.instruction: Identify the single word or short phrase that produces the laugh, then score its position. 10 = the loaded term is the final word of the caption and nothing follows it, so the caption stops the instant it detonates. 6 = the loaded term is in the final clause but followed by a few trailing words. 3 = the loaded term sits mid-caption and the caption continues past it with explanation or scene-setting. 0 = the loaded material is announced up front and the rest of the caption walks it back, softens it, or elaborates it. Score only placement; do not score how funny the term is.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high captions are almost uniformly end-loaded: R09 closes on 'herd immunity', R52 on 'vowel play', R35 on 'pooped', R22/R38 on 'no quarter' (dense .563-.994, card .028-.372). The dense-low side repeatedly spends its ending on aftermath rather than impact -- R17 ('oh, god. i think there's a theme') and R24 ('try howling like a wolf. it's hysterical') both trail off after the idea has already landed, yet score card .813/.888 against dense .128/.142. A bank built from readability and clarity criteria has no place to register where the payoff sits.

proposals.name: Both readings stay live simultaneously
proposals.instruction: Find any ambiguous word or phrase and test whether BOTH readings remain true of the situation the caption implies at the same time. 10 = a genuine double meaning where each sense is independently apt, so the caption cannot be reduced to one reading without losing something. 5 = a pun where the second sense is audible but only one sense actually fits the implied situation. 2 = a single-sense line with a mildly figurative word. 0 = wholly literal, no ambiguity available. Do not reward mere homophony; reward simultaneous truth of both senses.
proposals.rationale: R13 ('the gravity of our situation') and R37 ('the house has 88 keys and no locks') hold both senses at once and land at dense .824/.714 against card .233/.125; R41 ('never had a cross word between us') and R11 ('a two-step program') do the same at dense .702/.802, card .151/.287. Contrast the dense-low single-reading lines R29 ('i'm thinking takeout') and R25 ('i'm gonna eat dessert first'), card .871/.907 but dense .155/.338. A bank with a generic 'contains wordplay' item scores the two classes alike; the dense model is clearly grading the quality of the ambiguity, not its presence.

proposals.name: Institutional register deadpan over an absurd premise
proposals.instruction: Score the gap between the caption's diction and its content. 10 = the line is delivered in a flat professional, clinical, legal, corporate, or therapeutic register (performance review, policy language, negotiation, HR phrasing) with no acknowledgment that the situation is absurd. 5 = neutral everyday speech about an odd situation. 0 = the diction matches the silliness -- exclamatory, chatty, cute, or advertising-toned. High scores require the speaker to sound like they are on the clock.
proposals.rationale: R10 ('where we disagree is that exposed skin implies consent'), R11 ('entering a two-step program'), R14 ("all my evaluation said was 'good girl.'"), and R55 ('not discouraging words so much as constructive criticism') all adopt procedural diction and sit at dense .702-.859 with card .051-.287. The dense-low side is chatty or ad-toned: R40 ('perfect for a quick bite or an evening out') and R30 ('this hole-in-the-wall place you'll love') reach card .847/.938 on dense .268/.170. Fluency- and naturalness-style criteria reward the chatty voice; the register clash is invisible to them.

proposals.name: Unglossed allusion the reader must finish
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the joke is delegated to the reader's outside knowledge without any in-caption help. 10 = the caption quotes, twists, or truncates a song lyric, name, title, or stock phrase and never signals that it is doing so, so a reader who lacks the reference sees only a flat sentence. 5 = an allusion that is flagged or partly explained inside the caption. 0 = no outside reference required, or the reference is spelled out and its relevance stated. Score the withholding, not the obscurity.
proposals.rationale: R16 and R36 both bank silently on 'she'll be comin' round the mountain' (dense .951/.947, card .308/.155); R55 buries 'seldom is heard a discouraging word'; R07 ('wreckmaninoff') requires the composer's name with zero scaffolding at dense .794 / card .181. Compare dense-low R57 ('mass extinction is a really cool band name'), which states its own conceit outright, at card .924 / dense .021. A judge scoring self-containedness or intelligibility will penalize precisely the withholding the dense model rewards.

proposals.name: No self-commentary on its own funniness
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption stays inside its situation or steps out to appraise the joke. 0 = the caption labels its own material as amusing, ironic, thematic, or notable ('it's hysterical', 'that must be exciting', 'is a really cool band name', 'i think there's a theme'), or otherwise tells the reader how to react. 5 = mild evaluative language that could plausibly be in-character. 10 = the speaker is entirely absorbed in the situation and never comments on the humor; the line would be said the same way if it were not funny.
proposals.rationale: Four of the most card-favored items announce their own joke: R24 ('it's hysterical', card .888 / dense .142), R45 ('that must be exciting', card .730 / dense .065), R57 ('a really cool band name', card .924 / dense .021), R17 ('i think there's a theme', card .813 / dense .128). Nothing on the dense-high side does this -- R19, R43, and R59 simply state a fact and stop. A rubric with criteria about clarity of comic intent or signposting will actively credit the self-commentary that the dense model treats as a defect.

proposals.name: Implies a long prior history it never states
proposals.instruction: Score how much unstated backstory the caption forces the reader to reconstruct. 10 = the line presupposes an extensive prior situation -- an ongoing grievance, a running tally, a relationship with a history, a bureaucratic process already underway -- and states none of it, so the reader must build the world backwards from a single detail. 5 = a modest amount is implied, most is stated. 0 = the caption describes its own situation completely; nothing remains to be inferred. Score the ratio of implied to stated, not the plausibility of the world.
proposals.rationale: R06 ('581 days without an accident, and then you show up') and R33 ('you're very calm, given we had 500 this morning') both imply an entire prior run of events from one number, at dense .741/.880 versus card .119/.195; R19 ('he got indicted') and R43 ('they're still looking for votes') presuppose whole narratives in three or four words. The dense-low items narrate themselves instead: R02 ('i usually eat out back, but it's my birthday') and R30 lay out the full situation and reach card .879/.938 at dense .303/.170. Self-sufficiency criteria reward the narrated version.

proposals.name: Oddly specific number or proper noun carries the joke
proposals.instruction: Score the presence and comic function of precise particulars. 10 = a specific figure, count, or name is the pivot of the joke and a rounder or vaguer substitute would kill it. 6 = a specific particular is present and adds texture but the joke survives without it. 3 = only generic quantities ('some', 'a lot', 'a while'). 0 = no particulars at all, or a specific number that is purely decorative. Penalize specificity that is inert; reward specificity that is load-bearing.
proposals.rationale: The dense-high side is full of precision doing work: R06 ('581 days'), R28 ('45 pounds ... a leg'), R33 ('500 this morning'), R37 ('88 keys'), R21 ('100 wool') span dense .656-.949 against card .038-.433. The card-favored side is conspicuously vague: R29 ('i'm thinking takeout') and R25 ('eat dessert first') carry no particulars at all yet reach card .871/.907 on dense .155/.338. A bank scoring vividness or imagery in general terms will not distinguish load-bearing precision from ordinary description.

proposals.name: Transgressive content delivered without flinching
proposals.instruction: Score how far the caption goes into dark, cruel, sexual, morbid, or politically charged territory AND how flatly it delivers it. 10 = genuinely uncomfortable material stated in a completely level voice, with no softening, apology, or wink. 5 = mildly edgy material, or dark material that is immediately cushioned. 0 = entirely safe, agreeable, wholesome content. Judge tone and content jointly: edgy-but-hedged and flat-but-harmless both score mid or low. This scores comic nerve as observed in the text; do not score offensiveness as a defect.
proposals.rationale: R10 ('exposed skin implies consent'), R51 ('you should see the breasts'), R28 ('my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg'), and R06's flat insult all sit at dense .656-.929 with card .038-.130 -- among the widest gaps in the slice. The card-favored items are pointedly inoffensive: R40, R30, and R58 ('they think that we look alike too') are warm and safe at card .847/.938/.887 on dense .268/.170/.087. Any bank containing appropriateness, taste, or inclusiveness items will suppress the dense model's strongest signal here.

proposals.name: Topical reference does a second job beyond recognition
proposals.instruction: If the caption invokes a current event, political situation, or public-health moment, score whether the reference earns its place. 10 = the topical term is simultaneously doing non-topical work -- a pun, a character judgment, or a literal description of the implied situation -- so it would still function as a line even for a reader who missed the news. 5 = the reference is apt but does only one job. 0 = the reference is the entire joke; recognizing it is all that happens. Captions with no topical content are not applicable and should be scored 5.
proposals.rationale: This axis splits cleanly inside the slice. Dense-high topical items double up: R09 ('they claim they have herd immunity') is a pun on a literal herd, R19 ('he got indicted') is also a bare narrative fact, R43 ('they're still looking for votes') reads two ways, at dense .563/.957/.970 versus card .051/.389/.079. Dense-low topical items are recognition-only: R03 ('six feet dude. six. feet') and R23 ('of course, i'm vaccinated') just name the moment, at card .962/.582 on dense .040/.053. A single 'is it topical/relevant' criterion scores all five alike and gets the direction wrong on half of them.

proposals.name: Freshly minted versus stock borrowed formula
proposals.instruction: Score how newly made the joke feels. 10 = the construction appears to have been built for this situation; you cannot recall having heard the line or its template before. 5 = a familiar joke shape filled with fresh material. 0 = an off-the-shelf line, well-worn movie quote, or a joke template you have met many times ('what i'd really like to do is direct', 'having people for dinner', 'does this make me look big'). Judge familiarity of the construction, not familiarity of the subject matter.
proposals.rationale: The card-favored side is thick with recycled formulas: R12 ('i'm having people for dinner tonight'), R54 ('do you think it makes my teeth look big'), R39 ('what i'd really like to do is direct'), R46 ('what are we, neanderthals'), R25 ('eat dessert first') reach card .907-.994 while the dense model puts them at .036-.415. The dense-high side coins new material: R07, R52 ('i suspect vowel play'), R34 ('it's so ewe'). Well-formed stock lines score maximally on craft-style criteria -- clean grammar, clear mechanism, recognizable structure -- which is exactly what the scorecard appears to be over-crediting.

proposals.name: Throat-clearing before the joke
proposals.instruction: Score the amount of conversational preamble that precedes any comic content. 0 = the caption opens with discourse filler -- 'i don't know about you, but', 'believe it or not', 'on the plus side', 'enough about me', 'of course,', 'actually', 'i don't know.' -- that adds naturalness but no joke. 5 = a short functional lead-in that also sets up the payoff. 10 = the caption starts inside the joke with no runway at all. Score only the opening; a caption may be long and still open cold.
proposals.rationale: Nearly every heavily card-favored item opens with filler: R29 ('i don't know about you, but'), R58 ('believe it or not'), R57 ('on the plus side'), R45 ('enough about me'), R27 ('actually'), R54 ('i don't know.') run card .752-.938 against dense .036-.338. The dense-high items open cold: R19, R38 ('i will give you no quarter'), R34. Filler is precisely what makes a line read as authentic natural speech, so any naturalness or voice criterion will pay for it while the dense model charges for the wasted runway.

proposals.name: Label mode where the name itself is the joke
proposals.instruction: Some captions are not lines of dialogue but titles, labels, or namings of what is depicted. Score how well the caption commits to that mode. 10 = the caption is a bare label and the label itself is the entire joke -- a coinage, a renaming, or a deadpan category name that reframes the whole scene. 5 = a label with mild wit, or a line of dialogue that also functions as a title. 0 = a flat descriptive label with no torque. Captions that are clearly dialogue and nothing else should be scored 5 rather than penalized; do not deduct for the absence of a speaker.
proposals.rationale: Five of the widest dense-high gaps are non-dialogue labels: R07 ('wreckmaninoff', card .181), R60 ('republican primary ticket', card .034), R31 ('it's the republican slate of candidates', card .028), R47 ('welcome to the last resort', card .255), R53 ('our new white house collection', card .344), at dense .751-.922. Card scores in the .028-.344 band across all five, against a dense-low side made entirely of well-formed spoken lines, is the signature of a bank that requires the caption to sound like plausible character dialogue. That requirement is a category error for this mode.

proposals.name: Speaker asserts and acts, rather than asking and hedging
proposals.instruction: Score the speaker's stance toward the person addressed. 10 = a confident declarative that does something in the scene -- issues a threat, delivers a verdict, refuses, insults, or reframes the other party's position -- so the line changes the situation. 5 = a neutral observation or a question that carries real edge. 0 = a hedged question, a request for reassurance, or an agreeable pleasantry that leaves everything as it was. Score stance and force, not politeness.
proposals.rationale: The dense-high side is full of lines that act on the addressee: R38 ('i will give you no quarter'), R22 ('no. no quarter will be given'), R10 (a flat contradiction), R06 ('and then you show up'), R55 (a reframing) run dense .656-.994 at card .028-.372. The card-favored side asks and defers: R20 ('are you sure the boss is cool with this?'), R26 ('you're sure it's wild caught?'), R48 ('can i get a discount?'), R08 ('you seem really nice'), R45 all reach card .582-.781 on dense .028-.214. Well-formed polite dialogue reads as high-quality writing to a criterion bank while carrying no comic force.

proposals.name: Two joke systems firing at once
proposals.instruction: Count how many independent comic mechanisms the caption runs simultaneously -- e.g. a pun AND a coherent literal reading of the implied situation, or an allusion AND a character judgment, or a register clash AND a double meaning. 10 = at least two mechanisms are fully operative and each would be a passable joke alone, so they reinforce rather than merely coexist. 6 = two mechanisms but one is weak or decorative. 3 = one mechanism, cleanly executed. 0 = no identifiable mechanism beyond stating something mildly odd. Score the stacking, not the individual quality.
proposals.rationale: R09 ('they refuse to budge. they claim they have herd immunity') runs a literal herd, a public-health pun, and a stubbornness gag at once (dense .563 / card .051); R41 stacks the Holmes voice on the crossword pun (.702 / .151); R14 stacks a workplace performance review on a dog-praise reading (.827 / .170); R35 stacks fatigue on the literal reading of 'pooped' (.741 / .032). Single-mechanism card-favored items -- R44 ('the saturn ring toss'), R48 ('this fish is dead'), R29 -- sit at card .749-.820 on dense .097-.214. A bank that scores each property separately and then sums will credit two half-strength properties the same as one genuine stacking.

proposals.name: Terseness / token economy of the caption as written
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH brevity is present in the caption text, counting only what is written. 0 = long, 18+ words or several full sentences; 3 = roughly 13-17 words; 5 = roughly 9-12 words; 7 = roughly 5-8 words; 10 = extremely terse, a 1-4 word fragment or single coined word. Count words as whitespace-separated tokens. You are measuring observable length only. Do NOT judge whether the caption is funny, apt, clever, or good, and do NOT treat short or long as better; a maximally terse dud and a maximally terse gem both score 10.
proposals.rationale: Raw length separates the two disagreement arms almost mechanically: the dense-high/card-low arm is packed with one-to-five-word items (R39 'wreckmaninoff', R34 'it's so ewe', R47 'he got indicted', R04 'republican primary ticket', R15 'this is taking an eternity'), while the dense-low/card-high arm is dominated by long full utterances (R56 'i can usually identify a bird by the song, but i think he's doing a cover', R41 'are you sure the boss is cool with this? it took him six days to make', R10). Word count is a pure typographic quantity and carries no information about how good the caption is as a contest entry, but any bank of written criteria has more surface to grade on a long caption than a short one, so length will predict the scorecard's rank regardless of merit.

proposals.name: Standalone completeness: explicit referents, no picture needed
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption is a grammatically complete, self-parsing utterance whose participants and situation are named in the text itself rather than left to an unseen drawing. 0 = bare noun phrase or fragment with no finite verb and every referent supplied by the picture; 5 = a complete clause but with one or more bare deictics ('this', 'they', 'she', 'it') whose antecedent is not in the text; 10 = one or more complete sentences naming enough entities, roles or objects that a reader with no image can reconstruct who is speaking and about what. Score only observable syntactic completeness and referential explicitness. Do NOT judge whether the caption is good, and do NOT treat image-dependence as a flaw: a caption may be excellent precisely because it leans on the drawing.
proposals.rationale: This is the single cleanest fingerprint of the split and it is an artifact of the text-only reading condition, not of caption merit. R04 ('republican primary ticket') and R58 ('it's the republican slate of candidates') are fragments or bare deictics that mean nothing without the cartoon, and both sit in dense-high/card-low; R21 ('when did you first notice this personality change rabbi friedman') and R36 ('actually it's no dogs, cats or other small pets') name their own scene and both sit in dense-low/card-high. A criterion bank read against text alone can only find satisfied criteria in captions that carry their own context, so self-containment gets rewarded as if it were quality when it is really just legibility to a blind reader.

proposals.name: Bipartite setup-then-turn template with an explicit pivot
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the caption is built as a two-part construction: a first span that sets a frame, then a pivot at a comma, period, dash, colon or question mark, then a second span that redirects it. 0 = a single undivided span with no internal pivot; 5 = two spans joined but with a weak or purely additive pivot; 10 = a crisp two-beat structure with an explicit connective or punctuation break between the halves ('X, but Y', 'X? Y', 'X -- Y'). Score only the presence and clarity of the structural template. Do NOT judge whether the turn lands, is surprising, or is funny; a flat two-beat caption and a brilliant two-beat caption both score 10, and a brilliant single-span caption scores 0.
proposals.rationale: Template shape, not wit, tracks the arms: R06 ('we'll miss you bobby, but the dog is allergic'), R16 ('no bag--my cubs still think i catch my own salmon'), R54 and R56 all show the explicit two-beat pivot and all sit in dense-low/card-high; R15, R23, R34 and R53 are single undivided spans in dense-high/card-low. Written criteria decompose naturally into 'setup' and 'payoff' sub-checks, so a caption that visibly instantiates that shape collects credit on both, while an equally good caption whose whole joke is one compressed span can only be credited once. The shape is a compositional habit, not a property of how good the entry is.

proposals.name: Phonetic wordplay compressed into a single word
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of sound-based wordplay in the caption: homophones, near-homophones, portmanteaus, respellings, or an idiom whose ordinary meaning is displaced by a same-sounding alternative. 0 = no sound play, all words used in their plain sense; 5 = a mild double sense that does not depend on pronunciation; 10 = the caption's whole content is a phonetic substitution or coinage. Score only the presence and density of sound play as an observable linguistic operation. Do NOT judge whether the pun works, is groan-worthy, is original, or is good.
proposals.rationale: Pun-carrying items cluster hard in dense-high/card-low: R34 ('it's so ewe'), R39 ('wreckmaninoff'), R19 ('i suspect vowel play'), R44 ('could you pull the wool over my eyes'), R26 ('the gravity of our situation'), R60 ('88 keys and no locks'). A phonetic pun is a lexical mechanism, not a merit level -- puns range from superb to dire -- but it is nearly invisible to criteria written in propositional terms ('does the caption establish a situation', 'is there a reversal'), so its presence systematically depresses scorecard rank independently of quality. Declaring it a nuisance keeps 'contains a pun' out of the bank in both directions.

proposals.name: News-cycle and pandemic-era topical markers (MODE 2)
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the caption's content depends on a datable public event or news-cycle topic: electoral politics, indictments, administrations, public-health measures, distancing rules, vaccination, or similar period-specific public discourse. 0 = fully timeless content that would read identically in any decade; 5 = one glancing period-flavoured word; 10 = the caption is unintelligible without knowing a specific news topic current at the time of writing. Score only the observable presence of period-anchored topical reference. Do NOT judge whether the topicality is well used, timely, tasteful, or good.
proposals.rationale: When an entry was written is unobservable, but it leaves a heavy textual trace, and that trace concentrates in the dense-high/card-low arm: R04 ('republican primary ticket'), R58, R38 ('they're still looking for votes'), R47 ('he got indicted'), R28 ('our new white house collection'), and the distancing/immunity cluster R02 ('six feet dude. six. feet'), R13 ('they claim they have herd immunity'), R24 ('of course, i'm vaccinated'). Timing is a nuisance parent: an item's week determines what topical material was even available to it, which is not a fact about the writer's skill. Tagged mixed because a live topic can also genuinely sharpen a caption for its audience, so this must appear in both the discounted and undiscounted readouts.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing (which contest week / news cycle the entry was written in)

proposals.name: Borrowed cultural material: quoted lyrics, films, canon figures (MODE 2)
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption imports pre-existing cultural material rather than inventing its own phrasing: song lyrics, film or TV lines, literary or detective-fiction characters, composer or celebrity names, scripture or origin-myth motifs, well-known showbiz cliches. 0 = wholly original wording with no borrowed referent; 5 = one lightly evoked cultural referent; 10 = the caption is essentially a quotation or a direct riff on one recognisable source. Score only the amount of borrowed material detectable in the text. Do NOT judge whether the allusion is apt, well chosen, obscure, or good.
proposals.rationale: The unseen factor is who the writer is and what canon they carry; its fingerprint is which references appear at all. R20 and R30 both reach for the same folk-song lyric, R08 invokes Holmes and Watson, R39 rewrites Rachmaninoff, R09 ('i'm having people for dinner tonight') rides a famous film line, R07 quotes the 'what i'd really like to do is direct' showbiz cliche, R41 and R05 lean on origin-myth material. Repertoire access is a demographic accident, not a skill, yet a criterion bank containing anything like 'makes a recognisable cultural connection' converts cohort membership into score. Tagged mixed because a shared reference can also do genuine comic work for the readership.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's generational and cultural media repertoire (age cohort, education, reading and viewing history)

proposals.name: Reliance on the single most obvious stock hook for the scene (MODE 2)
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the caption's core turn rests on one widely-shared stock phrase -- an idiom, proverb, brand-level cliche, song title or fixed expression -- reused with little or no alteration, such that the phrase is doing the work rather than the caption's own construction. 0 = no fixed expression involved, the phrasing is built from scratch; 5 = a common expression present but substantially reworked or extended; 10 = the caption is a stock phrase lightly re-pointed at the scene. Score only the stock-ness and the degree of alteration of the phrase, both of which are visible in the text. Do NOT judge whether the caption is obvious, unoriginal, derivative, or good -- originality is explicitly out of scope for this channel.
proposals.rationale: Convergence is visible inside the slice itself: R20 and R30 are near-duplicate takes on the same folk-song hook, R46 ('no quarter will be given') and R53 ('i will give you no quarter') are near-duplicate takes on the same idiom, R04 and R58 restate the same ticket/slate hook, and R25, R34 and R44 all mine 'wool'. That duplication is a property of the shared prompt and the size of the entrant crowd, not of the individual writer, yet it moves both models: a stock phrase is easy for written criteria to recognise as 'a clean idiomatic turn'. Tagged mixed because low-alteration stock use plausibly bears on genuine merit too, so it must be reported as a sensitivity band rather than silently removed.
proposals.upstream_parent: crowd process dynamics: thousands of independent entrants working from one identical prompt converge on the same few available hooks

proposals.name: Proofing and typography artifacts: dashes, ellipses, terminal marks (MODE 2)
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of non-standard typographic and proofing artifacts visible in the caption: double-hyphen or spaced-hyphen dashes, multi-dot ellipses, stray or trailing punctuation, doubled spaces, missing or inconsistent terminal punctuation, run-on comma splices, unclosed quotation marks. Note that letter casing in this corpus appears to be normalised for every item, so IGNORE capitalisation entirely and score only dashes, dots, spacing, terminal marks and quote marks. 0 = clean, conventional punctuation throughout; 10 = several conspicuous artifacts or a visibly unedited trailing mark. Score only the observable typography. Do NOT judge whether the caption is careless, sloppy, polished, or good.
proposals.rationale: Whether an entry got a second read before being sent is unobservable but leaves punctuation residue. R51 carries both a four-dot ellipsis and a stray trailing double hyphen and sits at the extreme of the dense-high/card-low arm; R16 uses an unspaced double hyphen, R27 a spaced double hyphen and R59 a spaced single hyphen, and those three sit in dense-low/card-high with conventional sentence punctuation otherwise. Typography is not a fact about how good the caption is as a contest entry, and it is exactly the kind of visible residue a written-criteria bank picks up as 'well-formed'. Tagged mixed because the same editing pass that fixes punctuation may also have improved the joke.
proposals.upstream_parent: amount of composition care / editing pass before submission (and the submission interface used)

proposals.name: Venue-readership register: therapy, professions, in-laws, dining voice (MODE 2)
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the caption speaks in the domestic-professional register of a metropolitan magazine readership: therapy and analysis talk, white-collar job titles, clergy or professional honorifics, in-law and spouse relations, dating talk, restaurant and food-shopping vocabulary, consumer-brand and provenance talk, office and workplace idiom. 0 = none of this register, the diction is neutral or belongs to some other world; 5 = one such marker in passing; 10 = the caption is entirely built out of this register's vocabulary and situations. Score only the observable presence of these register markers. Do NOT judge whether the register is used well, whether it suits the scene, or whether the caption is good.
proposals.rationale: Fit with the venue's audience is an unobservable property of the writer, but its fingerprint is the diction. The dense-low/card-high arm is saturated with it: R21 ('when did you first notice this personality change rabbi friedman'), R42 ('you're an accountant? that must be exciting'), R31 ('i let your father shop at costco'), R54 ('you're sure it's wild caught? my in-laws can tell'), R10 and R27 (restaurant-review voice), R59 (dating talk). The dense-high/card-low arm rarely uses it. Sounding like the readership is a matter of social positioning rather than craft, yet criteria written by or for that readership will read the house voice as competence. Tagged mixed because venue fluency plausibly does raise real fit for the audience as well.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's demographic and cultural fit with the venue's readership (which determines fluency in the house voice)

proposals.name: Off-colour, bodily and dark-subject content
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of transgressive content in the caption: sexual or anatomical reference, consent or harassment themes, bodily-function or scatological words, bodily harm, death, cannibalism, or cruelty toward a named party. 0 = wholly innocuous content; 5 = one mild edgy or bodily word; 10 = the caption's central content is sexual, scatological, violent or otherwise taboo. Score only the observable presence and intensity of such content. Do NOT judge whether the transgression is funny, gratuitous, offensive, well-handled, or good, and do NOT reward or penalise edginess; you are counting content type only.
proposals.rationale: Transgressive content concentrates in the dense-high/card-low arm: R33 ('where we disagree is that exposed skin implies consent'), R48 ('you should see the breasts'), R40 ('we'll be pooped by the end of the night'), R17 ('my dad lost a leg'), with R06 and R09 carrying darker material on the other arm. Content category is orthogonal to how good the caption is as a contest entry -- taboo captions span the full merit range -- but explicit criteria almost always carry an implicit propriety filter, so this material is penalised or bonused as a class. Declaring it a nuisance prevents 'is it clean' and 'is it daring' from entering the bank under either sign.

proposals.name: Literalized reuse of a known idiom or fixed phrase
proposals.instruction: Score how precisely the caption takes a widely recognizable idiom, song lyric, or set phrase and repurposes it (often literally) to fit the depicted scene. 10 = the caption is built entirely around a well-known phrase whose reused meaning maps cleanly and surprisingly onto the new context; 0 = the caption uses no recognizable fixed phrase, only original wording.
proposals.rationale: R18 and R32 independently reuse the exact same folk-song lyric ('coming round the mountain') recontextualized as a breakup/euphemism line, and R34/R51 both independently reuse the archaic phrase 'no quarter' - the same underlying joke concept recurring across different phrasings, both dense_high_card_low, suggests the dense model rewards this device specifically while the scorecard misses it. R33 ('pull the wool over my eyes') and R56 ('cross word between us') show the same pattern.

proposals.name: Punchline economy with no throat-clearing setup
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the caption is pure comedic payload versus preamble, wind-up, or filler. 10 = a short, self-contained line where essentially every word is doing comedic work with no wasted setup; 0 = a long lead-in or multiple clauses of table-setting before (or instead of) any punch.
proposals.rationale: R28 ('he got indicted', 3 words) and R45 ('this is taking an eternity', 5 words) are both dense_high_card_low despite near-total absence of setup, while dense_low_card_high items like R01 ('are you sure the boss is cool with this? it took him six days to make') and R08 carry substantially more preliminary clauses before any twist lands.

proposals.name: Clean phonetic/sound-alike wordplay transformation
proposals.instruction: Score the craft of any pun built on swapping a sound-alike word or phrase for the expected one. 10 = an immediately parseable, clean phonetic substitution where the new word both sounds right and re-signifies the scene (e.g. a homophone swap); 0 = no phonetic wordplay present, or a pun so strained it barely lands.
proposals.rationale: R05 ('i suspect vowel play', foul play -> vowel play) and R11 ('it's so ewe', you -> ewe) and R23 ('wreckmaninoff', wreck + Rachmaninoff) are all dense_high_card_low and hinge entirely on tight phonetic substitution, a device the card-based items (e.g. R41, R60) largely lack.

proposals.name: Deadpan unhedged declarative delivery
proposals.instruction: Score how flatly assertive and unqualified the caption's delivery is. 10 = a blunt, confident declarative statement (or short fragment) with no hedging language; 0 = the line is phrased as a question, or is softened with hedges like 'i don't know', 'are you sure', 'do you think'.
proposals.rationale: R34 ('No. No quarter will be given') and R28 ('he got indicted') are terse, unhedged assertions and both dense_high_card_low, while R01 ('are you sure the boss is cool with this?'), R07 ('do you think i'm crazy'), and R15 ('do you think it makes my teeth look big') are all hedged/interrogative and dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Directness on taboo or transgressive subject matter
proposals.instruction: Score how directly the caption confronts dark, risque, or uncomfortable content rather than softening or avoiding it. 10 = the caption states taboo or edgy content plainly, with no cushioning; 0 = the content is entirely safe, warm, or family-friendly with no edge.
proposals.rationale: R06 ('you should see the breasts') and R26 ('exposed skin implies consent') and R47 ('my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg') are all dense_high_card_low and confront blunt/dark material head-on, in contrast to gentler dense_low_card_high items like R12 ('try howling like a wolf, it's hysterical') or R60.

proposals.name: Absurdly precise invented numeric detail
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption invents a specific, oddly precise number purely for comic effect. 10 = a hyper-specific, non-round number is central to the joke's absurdity; 0 = no numeric detail, or only a vague/generic quantity.
proposals.rationale: R04 ('581 days without an accident') and R13 ('given we had 500 this morning') and R40 ('now the house has 88 keys and no locks') are all dense_high_card_low and use an oddly exact number as the comic engine, a device largely absent from dense_low_card_high items like R41.

proposals.name: Clash between elevated/formal diction and mundane scene
proposals.instruction: Score the degree of register mismatch between the caption's vocabulary and the ordinary or absurd situation it describes. 10 = formal, archaic, legalistic, or technical diction is applied to a mundane/absurd scene for comic contrast; 0 = the diction is uniformly casual/plain throughout, matching the scene register.
proposals.rationale: R34/R51 use the archaic military phrase 'no quarter', R56 uses the Victorian-Holmesian 'cross word between us', and R26 uses legalistic phrasing ('implies consent') - all dense_high_card_low - producing a register clash the scorecard appears to undervalue relative to more register-flat dense_low_card_high lines.

proposals.name: Originality versus a recognizable stock joke template
proposals.instruction: Score how original the caption's underlying joke structure is, versus how much it matches a widely recognized, formulaic internet/meme joke template. 10 = a fully original construction not traceable to a known joke format; 0 = the caption is instantly recognizable as a stock template filled in with scene-specific nouns.
proposals.rationale: R44 ('mass extinction is a really cool band name') follows the extremely common 'X would be a great band name' meme template and is dense_low_card_high despite scoring high with the scorecard; R17 ('i think there's a theme') is a similarly generic meta-observation and also dense_low_card_high, while more original constructions like R23 ('wreckmaninoff') are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Non-redundant economy, no repetition-as-emphasis crutch
proposals.instruction: Score whether every clause of the caption introduces new information versus repeating a word/phrase purely for emphasis. 10 = no repeated words or restatements, each clause advances the joke; 0 = the caption leans on repeating the same word or phrase as a substitute for a real punchline.
proposals.rationale: R09 ('six feet dude. six. feet') repeats 'six feet' as its primary device and is dense_low_card_high, in contrast to single-shot, non-repetitive dense_high_card_low lines like R45 ('this is taking an eternity') and R28 ('he got indicted').

proposals.name: Standalone quotability without needing the unseen image
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption reads as a complete, funny line on its own, without requiring the (unseen) cartoon's visual to supply missing context. 10 = fully self-contained as a one-liner, funny even quoted in isolation; 0 = flat or uninterpretable without the accompanying image/scene.
proposals.rationale: R28 ('he got indicted') and R51 ('i will give you no quarter') are dense_high_card_low and work as free-standing lines, whereas R41 ('actually it's no dogs, cats or other small pets') and R03 ('love it -- perfect for a quick bite or an evening out') are dense_low_card_high but read as inert, generic text without a scene to anchor them.

proposals.name: Naturalistic, distinct character voice in the dialogue
proposals.instruction: Score how convincingly the caption reads as something a specific, believable person would actually say aloud in the depicted moment, with authentic conversational rhythm. 10 = fully convincing as overheard real speech with a distinct persona; 0 = stilted, generic, or written like copy rather than spoken dialogue.
proposals.rationale: R52 ('enough about me. you're an accountant? that must be exciting') and R55 ('if you're free after work, i know this hole-in-the-wall place you'll love') and R31 ('no bag--my cubs still think i catch my own salmon') are all dense_low_card_high and read as highly naturalistic overheard dialogue, a quality the scorecard seems to reward more than the dense model does.

proposals.name: Convincing pastiche of a real-world text genre
proposals.instruction: Score how well the caption imitates the voice of a specific real-world non-conversational text genre (ad copy, product label, review, posted sign, etc.) rather than reading as spoken dialogue. 10 = convincingly mimics a recognizable real-world text genre; 0 = reads as ordinary conversational speech with no genre mimicry.
proposals.rationale: R03 ('love it -- perfect for a quick bite or an evening out') mimics restaurant-review/ad copy and R41 ('actually it's no dogs, cats or other small pets') mimics posted-sign language - both dense_low_card_high - suggesting the scorecard rewards this genre-pastiche technique more than the dense model does.

proposals.name: Topical reference bent into a new angle, not restated
proposals.instruction: Score whether a real-world topical or cultural reference (politics, pandemic terminology, etc.) is transformed into an unexpected new comedic angle, versus simply stated at face value. 10 = the topical reference is twisted into a genuinely new joke; 0 = the topical fact is stated plainly with no reinterpretation.
proposals.rationale: R30 ('they claim they have herd immunity') puns the pandemic term into a literal animal-herd joke and is dense_high_card_low, alongside political terms sharpened into one-liners in R14, R28, R37, R48, and R50 (all dense_high_card_low); by contrast R07 ('of course, i'm vaccinated. do you think i'm crazy') states the same topical territory fairly directly and is dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Sustained double meaning across the whole line
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption's key words operate on two simultaneous levels of meaning across the entire line, versus containing only one clever word embedded in an otherwise single-register sentence. 10 = the whole caption sustains a coherent double reading start to finish; 0 = purely literal, single-register meaning throughout.
proposals.rationale: R33 ('could you pull the wool over my eyes') and R46 ('i love that it's 100 wool') both sustain a literal-sheep/idiomatic double reading across the full line and are dense_high_card_low, compared to single-register lines like R60 ('in that case, i'm gonna eat dessert first') which is dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Late twist or escalation in the final clause
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption sets up an expectation early and then overturns or sharpens it in its closing words, producing a distinct turn. 10 = a clear rug-pull or sharpening twist lands specifically at the end of the line; 0 = the caption proceeds as one flat, predictable statement with no turn.
proposals.rationale: R04 ('581 days without an accident, and then you show up') turns sharply on its final clause and R47 ('my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg') turns on its second half - both dense_high_card_low - versus single-beat lines like R60 ('in that case, i'm gonna eat dessert first', dense_low_card_high) which build to no comparable late turn.

proposals.name: Caption brevity / low word count
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how terse/minimal the caption is as a standalone string: 0 = a long, multi-clause sentence; 10 = a single word or very short phrase (four words or fewer) with no subordinate clauses. Score only the raw word/character economy of the text; do NOT judge whether the brevity makes the caption funnier or better-suited to the image.
proposals.rationale: Very short entries cluster on one side: R08 'wreckmaninoff' (one word, dense_pct=0.794, card_pct=0.181) and R51 'it's so ewe' (three words, dense_pct=0.981, card_pct=0.185) sit far out dense-high/card-low, while long multi-clause entries like R22 'i don't know. do you think it makes my teeth look big' (dense_pct=0.214, card_pct=0.958) and R30 'it's an appetizer. i'm having people for dinner tonight' (dense_pct=0.360, card_pct=0.994) sit dense-low/card-high — a raw length confound, not necessarily fit-to-image quality.

proposals.name: Reliance on a stock idiom or catchphrase
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption's entire comic payload consists of a single well-known idiom, song lyric, or fixed phrase used with little or no alteration (for example a familiar saying about mercy, a folk-song line, or a common eyes/wool expression). 0 = no recognizable fixed phrase is used; 10 = the caption IS the fixed phrase, essentially verbatim. Score only whether a well-known stock phrase is present and how central it is to the line; do not judge whether the reuse is clever or funny.
proposals.rationale: R37 'it's time to accept that she's never coming round the mountain' (dense_pct=0.951, card_pct=0.308) and R47 'i think we need to face the possibility that she won't be comin' round the mountain' (dense_pct=0.947, card_pct=0.155) are two near-duplicate riffs on the same folk-song idiom, both far out on the same side; R48 'no. no quarter will be given' (dense_pct=0.945, card_pct=0.253) and R60 'i will give you no quarter' (dense_pct=0.994, card_pct=0.372) show the same phrase recycled twice more, suggesting shared-prompt convergence rather than independent per-caption quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: shared visual prompt driving convergent, independently-arrived-at ideas among many entrants (anchoring on the same obvious idiom)

proposals.name: Hyperbolic precise-numeral detail
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption relies on a specific, non-round numeral (such as an odd count of days, keys, or degrees) stated as a precise fact for comic exaggeration. 0 = no numerals appear; 10 = a precise number is the central comic device of the line. Score only the presence/centrality of a precise numeral, not whether the joke built on it lands.
proposals.rationale: R06 'now the house has 88 keys and no locks' (dense_pct=0.714, card_pct=0.125) and R32 '581 days without an accident, and then you show up' (dense_pct=0.741, card_pct=0.119), plus R56 'you're very calm, given we had 500 this morning' (dense_pct=0.880, card_pct=0.195), all lean on an oddly precise numeral and all three cluster dense-high/card-low.

proposals.name: Named political-party or election vocabulary
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption uses explicit political-party, election, or legal-jeopardy vocabulary (terms naming a party, a primary or slate of candidates, votes, an indictment, or a seat of government). 0 = no such vocabulary; 10 = the caption is built entirely around named political-process terms. Score only the presence of this vocabulary, not whether the political joke is insightful or funny.
proposals.rationale: R02 'it's the republican slate of candidates' (dense_pct=0.764, card_pct=0.028), R23 'republican primary ticket' (dense_pct=0.751, card_pct=0.034), R27 'he got indicted' (dense_pct=0.957, card_pct=0.389), and R49 'they're still looking for votes' (dense_pct=0.970, card_pct=0.079) are four separate political/news captions that all fall in dense_high_card_low.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing relative to a specific real-world news cycle (an election season, an indictment, etc.)

proposals.name: Pandemic or geopolitical event-pinning vocabulary
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption references a specific, dateable real-world event or era outside party politics — such as vaccination status, a named ongoing war or invasion, or other period-specific current-events shorthand. 0 = no such reference; 10 = the caption's premise depends entirely on that event being current. Score only the presence of such era-pinning content, not whether the reference is used cleverly.
proposals.rationale: R24 'of course, i'm vaccinated. do you think i'm crazy' (dense_pct=0.053, card_pct=0.582) and R39 'let's go. mommy doesn't have enough quarters to invade russia' (dense_pct=0.322, card_pct=0.898) both pin the joke to a specific era's news and both land in dense_low_card_high, a distinct cluster from the party-politics cases in B04.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing pinned to a specific real-world event or era (pandemic, geopolitical conflict) rather than a timeless reading of the cartoon

proposals.name: Workplace performance-review vocabulary
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption uses explicit formal-workplace evaluation vocabulary — words like an official evaluation, criticism framed as constructive, or references to a boss or performance review — as if describing an office review process. 0 = none present; 10 = the entire caption is phrased as workplace-review language. Score only the presence of this register, not whether the joke about being evaluated is funny.
proposals.rationale: R35 'all my evaluation said was good girl.' (dense_pct=0.827, card_pct=0.170) and R59 'don't think of them as discouraging words so much as constructive criticism' (dense_pct=0.773, card_pct=0.206) both explicitly borrow office-review vocabulary and both sit dense_high_card_low; R18 'are you sure the boss is cool with this? it took him six days to make' (dense_pct=0.028, card_pct=0.563) shows the same workplace-authority framing recurring on the opposite side of the disagreement, indicating this register is a recurring, direction-independent fingerprint in the slice rather than incidental.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's professional or institutional exposure to formal performance-review culture, leaving a jargon fingerprint in the text

proposals.name: Risqué or taboo bodily content
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption invokes taboo, risqué, or body-focused content (nudity, anatomy, sexual innuendo, or consent language) rather than a neutral, family-safe frame. 0 = entirely neutral; 10 = the caption's central content is taboo/risqué. Score only the presence of such content, not whether the risqué joke is tasteful or funny.
proposals.rationale: R01 'where we disagree is that exposed skin implies consent' (dense_pct=0.859, card_pct=0.038) and R54 'you should see the breasts' (dense_pct=0.929, card_pct=0.070) are both taboo/body-focused captions that cluster tightly in dense_high_card_low with very low card_pct.
proposals.upstream_parent: curation/engagement dynamics on the receiving side, where taboo or provocative content draws disproportionate attention or discussion independent of comic craft

proposals.name: Reassurance/excuse question-answer dialogue template
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption follows a stock reassurance-or-excuse conversational template — a rhetorical question about being judged, followed by a deflecting or minimizing answer (e.g. an 'of course' opener, or a 'do you think X' tag question). 0 = no such template; 10 = the caption is structured entirely as this kind of exchange. Score only whether this conversational shape is present, not whether the exchange is witty.
proposals.rationale: R22 'i don't know. do you think it makes my teeth look big' (dense_pct=0.214, card_pct=0.958), R24 'of course, i'm vaccinated. do you think i'm crazy' (dense_pct=0.053, card_pct=0.582), and R53 'you seem really nice - most of the guys i date are clowns' (dense_pct=0.161, card_pct=0.711) all use this reassurance/deflection shape and all sit dense_low_card_high; the shape is a formal template rather than an indicator of fit to the image.

proposals.name: Genre-pastiche of a non-cartoon written register
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption mimics the fixed phrasing conventions of a specific, unrelated written genre — e.g. a restaurant review, a real-estate listing, or a dating-app message — rather than reading as spontaneous spoken dialogue. 0 = no genre mimicry; 10 = the caption reads as if lifted directly from that other genre. Score only the presence of the borrowed register, not whether the pastiche is executed well.
proposals.rationale: R55 'love it -- perfect for a quick bite or an evening out' (dense_pct=0.268, card_pct=0.847) reads like restaurant-review copy, and R58 'if you're free after work, i know this hole-in-the-wall place you'll love' (dense_pct=0.170, card_pct=0.938) reads like a dating-app pitch — both genre-pastiche lines sit in dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Staccato repetition or fragmenting punctuation
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption uses repeated short clauses, sentence fragments, or unusual punctuation (ellipses, an isolated single word set off by a period, trailing dashes) purely for rhythmic emphasis. 0 = normal single-clause punctuation; 10 = heavy fragmenting/repetition for emphasis. Score only the presence of this typographic/rhythmic device, not whether the emphasis is effective.
proposals.rationale: R25 'six feet dude. six. feet' (dense_pct=0.040, card_pct=0.962) fragments the same two words three times for emphasis, and R07 'the difference between let's eat, chefs! and let's eat chefs! is not as subtle as one would think.... --' (dense_pct=0.563, card_pct=0.017) uses trailing ellipsis-and-dash punctuation — both show unusual fragmenting/punctuation choices that are formal, not content-based.

proposals.name: Compressed comic economy
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when very few words establish a situation and deliver a complete payoff; score 0 when the wording is bloated, fragmentary, or lacks a discernible payoff.
proposals.rationale: R05 and R40 achieve substantial humor through extremely compressed wording, while longer explanatory lines such as R18 and R21 show the contrasting risk.

proposals.name: Dual-use anchor word
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a central word naturally supports both a literal reading and a second figurative or thematic reading; score 0 when each word has only one usable meaning.
proposals.rationale: R05 uses “keys,” R23 uses “gravity,” and R49 uses “resort” as compact semantic pivots with multiple readings.

proposals.name: Phonetic pun precision
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a sound-alike, spelling shift, or pronunciation-based substitution is exact and immediately intelligible; score 0 when the sound connection is forced or unclear.
proposals.rationale: R12, R38, and R40 show tightly targeted sound-based transformations rather than merely adjacent words.

proposals.name: Micro-level wording payoff
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a tiny change in punctuation, repetition, or grammatical framing substantially changes the meaning or comic force; score 0 when such wording details are interchangeable.
proposals.rationale: R13 derives its mechanism from punctuation and sentence segmentation, while R37 uses repetition and phrasing to intensify “no quarter.”

proposals.name: Idiom re-engineering
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a familiar idiom is deliberately recast to fit a concrete situation and gains a new meaning; score 0 when the idiom is quoted conventionally without transformation.
proposals.rationale: R41, R42, and R44 actively reshape familiar expressions, whereas a stock phrase would provide recognition without much invention.

proposals.name: Active cultural allusion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a cultural, historical, or political reference is essential to the joke’s mechanism and is freshly repurposed; score 0 when it is merely a topical label or name-drop.
proposals.rationale: R16 and R55 use political terminology as the structural engine, while R43 turns a recognizable literary reference into a linguistic twist.

proposals.name: Late-clause reinterpretation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the ending sharply revises the reader’s interpretation of the opening rather than simply adding information; score 0 when the caption remains semantically flat from start to finish.
proposals.rationale: R06, R19, and R60 each withhold the decisive interpretation until the latter part of the sentence.

proposals.name: Distinctive interpersonal voice
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the speaker’s attitude, relationship, or power dynamic is vivid and specific; score 0 when the line could be spoken by anyone without changing its effect.
proposals.rationale: R06 and R31 imply sharply characterized speaker relationships, unlike generic conversational remarks such as R21.

proposals.name: Controlled edgy incongruity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when dark, sexual, political, or otherwise risky material is handled through a precise conceptual twist; score 0 when provocation is present without an inventive mechanism.
proposals.rationale: R27, R52, and R60 use potentially provocative material in structurally distinct ways rather than relying solely on shock.

proposals.name: Coherent absurdity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an impossible premise follows a clear internal logic that the reader can reconstruct; score 0 when the absurdity feels arbitrary or disconnected.
proposals.rationale: R09 and R48 build bizarre situations around understandable rules, while R26 illustrates how an unusual premise can become less coherent.

proposals.name: Conversational quotability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption sounds like a natural spoken line with strong rhythm and a crisp final beat; score 0 when it sounds stiff, over-explained, or difficult to say aloud.
proposals.rationale: R08 and R42 have compact, performable cadence, while R18 and R30 are more dependent on explanatory setup.

proposals.name: Scene-specific concreteness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when concrete objects, roles, or circumstances make the implied scene unmistakably specific; score 0 when the line is generic banter or interchangeable filler.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R39 supply distinctive concrete anchors, whereas R28, R34, and R57 could fit many unrelated scenes.

proposals.name: Freshness of comic mechanism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption combines familiar materials in an uncommon, non-template way; score 0 when it relies on a predictable pun, cliché, or standard joke pattern.
proposals.rationale: R40 and R43 use unusually specific mechanisms, while R11 and R24 illustrate more readily recognizable wordplay templates.

proposals.name: Implied rather than explained
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the reader must make a rewarding inference and the caption trusts that inference; score 0 when it announces, labels, or explains its own joke.
proposals.rationale: R13 and R31 leave the key connection for the reader to infer, whereas R50 explicitly announces that a theme exists.

proposals.name: Exact premise-punchline fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the punchline is an unusually precise response to the implied situation and depends on its details; score 0 when the same punchline could be attached to almost any premise.
proposals.rationale: R05 and R20 tightly bind wording to their implied situations, while R26 and R59 use lines whose applicability is comparatively broad.

proposals.name: Caption verbosity
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, score only how much length, clause structure, and explanatory material the text contains; do not judge whether the caption is good, funny, clever, or otherwise high-quality.
proposals.rationale: Length and elaboration may act as superficial effort or readability signals without measuring contest merit. Compare the compact R05 with the more elaborated R12 and R17.

proposals.name: Current-affairs topicality
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, score only the extent of explicit references to contemporary politics, public institutions, or current public events; do not judge whether those references improve the caption.
proposals.rationale: Submission timing can make topical references unusually salient even when topicality is unrelated to intrinsic caption quality. Examples include R07, R14, R19, and R51.

proposals.name: Animal vocabulary
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, score only how much the text refers to animals, pets, livestock, wildlife, or animal behavior; do not judge whether the animal material is amusing or effective.
proposals.rationale: Animal language may correlate with recurring cartoon subjects or venue conventions without indicating entry quality. Examples include R01, R03, R25, R36, R55, and R59.

proposals.name: Cultural specificity
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, score only the extent of named people, brands, places, groups, media, or other culturally specific references; do not judge whether the references are apt or funny.
proposals.rationale: An author's network or assumed audience may shape which recognizable references appear, independently of quality; the same cultural fluency may also enable genuinely stronger work. Examples include R20, R25, R30, and R31.
proposals.upstream_parent: author cultural network or audience familiarity

proposals.name: Sensitive bodily language
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, score only the extent of anatomical, sexual, bodily-harm, or bodily-risk language; do not judge whether the feature is appropriate, offensive, or effective.
proposals.rationale: Social or moderation sensitivities can make bodily wording consequential without making it a quality attribute. Examples include R13, R28, R46, and R56.

proposals.name: Stock dialogue scaffolding
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, score only how much the caption uses familiar conversational setups, such as greetings, invitations, disclaimers, or routine dialogue openers; do not judge whether the setup works.
proposals.rationale: Editing or coaching may encourage standardized conversational templates that affect textual reception; coaching can also sometimes improve genuine execution. Examples include R26, R35, R47, and R60.

proposals.name: Typing and formatting signature
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, score only the extent of fragments, repeated punctuation, unusual dashes, shorthand, contractions, or other visible typing and formatting habits; do not judge whether the presentation is good.
proposals.rationale: Interface conventions or hurried entry conditions can leave formatting traces that a text model notices without representing caption quality. Examples include R12, R25, R29, and R46.

proposals.name: Numerical detail density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, score only how much the text contains explicit numbers, measurements, durations, counts, or quantified detail; do not judge whether the specificity strengthens the caption.
proposals.rationale: Detailed source access may produce numerical fingerprints that influence textual modeling, while richer source information could also support genuinely better work. Examples include R13, R22, R34, R41, R46, and R57.
proposals.upstream_parent: access to detailed visual prompt or source material

proposals.name: Question and address framing
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, score only the extent of interrogatives, commands, and direct second-person address; do not judge whether the conversational framing is engaging or effective.
proposals.rationale: Question-heavy or directly addressed wording may trigger generic conversational associations without measuring quality. Examples include R04, R10, R20, R26, and R41.

proposals.name: Phonetic wordplay markers
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, score only the extent of homophones, sound substitutions, pun-like spellings, or explicit references to word sounds; do not judge whether the wordplay is clever or successful.
proposals.rationale: Specialized authors or coaching may leave recognizable wordplay markers that correlate with reception independently of execution; wordplay expertise can also contribute to genuine quality. Examples include R03, R16, R36, and R39.
proposals.upstream_parent: author genre specialization or caption-contest coaching

proposals.name: Compactness with payload
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when every word advances the setup, reinterpretation, or punchline and nothing feels expendable; score 0 when padding, repetition, or excess wording weakens the joke.
proposals.rationale: The terse, forceful constructions in R09 and R46 contrast with the more generic conversational phrasing in R22 and R44.

proposals.name: Idiomatic frame transformation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a familiar idiom, title, proverb, or lyric is recognizable but altered into a fresh, situation-specific meaning; score 0 when no such frame exists or it is merely repeated.
proposals.rationale: R06, R25, and R48 preserve recognizable phrases while redirecting them, a pattern underrepresented by more literal lines such as R34.

proposals.name: Exact wordplay fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a homophone, near-homophone, spelling shift, or lexical substitution is precise and semantically apt; score 0 when there is no wordplay or the resemblance feels strained.
proposals.rationale: R47, R50, and R60 rely on compact sound or spelling transformations, whereas several card-favored lines use looser associations.

proposals.name: Dual-reading payoff
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when one phrase cleanly supports two distinct readings and both contribute materially to the humor; score 0 when it has only one reading or the ambiguity adds nothing.
proposals.rationale: R04 exploits both musical keys and locks, while R10 and R16 similarly make one expression operate in two coherent domains.

proposals.name: Delayed reinterpretation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the opening invites an ordinary interpretation and the ending makes the reader revise it; score 0 when the premise and punch are immediately obvious or disconnected.
proposals.rationale: R17 and R24 withhold the decisive interpretation until late, as does the reversal in R55; this structural timing is not captured by surface topicality alone.

proposals.name: Meaningful numerical specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an exact number, count, or measurement makes the premise vivid and intensifies the joke; score 0 when numerical detail is absent, arbitrary, or irrelevant.
proposals.rationale: The quantities in R26, R27, and R55 create distinctive comic premises rather than generic situations.

proposals.name: Vivid scene specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption evokes a concrete, unusual scene with identifiable roles, objects, and actions; score 0 when it could be pasted into many unrelated scenes without change.
proposals.rationale: R27 and R57 imply sharply particular situations, while R22 and R34 rely on broadly reusable restaurant or invitation language.

proposals.name: Controlled tonal collision
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a serious, formal, or moral register collides deliberately and coherently with an absurd situation; score 0 when the tonal mismatch is random, merely topical, or confusing.
proposals.rationale: R08, R40, and R45 derive force from controlled clashes between grave language and comic circumstances.

proposals.name: Ending leverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the final word or phrase completes the syntax and sharply recasts the preceding material; score 0 when the ending could be removed or replaced with little loss.
proposals.rationale: R15, R37, and R59 place substantial comic force in the final word or phrase.

proposals.name: Distinctive speaker voice
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when diction reveals a particular speaker’s attitude, role, or personality and would not sound interchangeable; score 0 when the voice is generic and characterless.
proposals.rationale: R06’s faux-Watson diction, R17’s managerial euphemism, and R24’s evaluative pet-command voice show strongly differentiated speakers.

proposals.name: Freshness over stockness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the premise and wording take an uncommon route and avoid familiar joke templates; score 0 when the line is canned banter, a predictable invitation, or a stock pun.
proposals.rationale: R22, R34, R42, and R44 use highly reusable conversational formulas, suggesting a property that can distinguish surface plausibility from originality.

proposals.name: Self-contained intelligibility
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the joke’s referents, premise, and turn can be understood from the caption alone; score 0 when it is an unexplained fragment or depends heavily on missing context.
proposals.rationale: R29 and R43 provide little standalone setup, while R50 illustrates how even an unusual reference can still signal a decipherable wordplay mechanism.

proposals.name: Coherent causal twist
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the punch follows from a surprising but inferable chain of implications; score 0 when it is only a topical association, arbitrary juxtaposition, or non sequitur.
proposals.rationale: R31 and R39 connect their premises to loosely related punchlines, whereas R57 and R55 make their unexpected turns more causally legible.

proposals.name: Punctuation as comic timing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when punctuation, spacing, repetition, or word order intentionally controls alternate meaning and timing; score 0 when such mechanics are absent or awkward enough to obscure the joke.
proposals.rationale: R18 makes punctuation determine the meaning, and R29 uses repetition and pauses as part of its delivery.

proposals.name: Disproportionate consequence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a modest premise escalates into an unexpected, concrete, and disproportionate consequence that remains logically connected; score 0 when there is no consequence or the outcome is routine.
proposals.rationale: R27 escalates a routine safety record into an accusatory arrival, while R55 turns an ordinary weight-loss report into a startling physical-loss contrast.

proposals.name: Phonetic wordplay
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of puns, homophones, respellings, or sound-based wordplay. Judge only presence and extent; do not judge whether it is good.
proposals.rationale: This visible stylistic habit may correlate with reception while being separable from overall contest quality. Examples include R01, R11, R43, and R58.

proposals.name: Familiar allusions
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of familiar idioms, quotations, songs, fictional figures, or pre-existing cultural phrasing. Judge only reference presence; do not judge whether it is good or apt.
proposals.rationale: Recognizable cultural material can trigger predictable responses independently of caption quality. Examples include R05, R28, R46, and R55.

proposals.name: Time-bound topicality
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of references to time-sensitive public-affairs, health, or political topics. Judge only explicit topicality; do not judge whether it is good or relevant.
proposals.rationale: Submission timing can leave traces through contemporaneous vocabulary, which may affect reception without improving the text itself. Examples include R06, R18, R47, and R50.

proposals.name: Copyediting normalization
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of standardized punctuation, spacing, capitalization, apostrophe, and sentence-format conventions. Judge only visible editing conventions; do not judge whether the result is good.
proposals.rationale: Professional editing can create recognizable textual polish and can also genuinely improve wording, so this is a sensitivity channel. Examples include R02, R11, R44, and R57.

proposals.name: Named-entity density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of specific proper names, brands, institutions, or uniquely identifying entities. Judge only specificity and density; do not judge whether the references are good.
proposals.rationale: Network or institutional access may supply distinctive names and contexts that influence reception, while sometimes also supplying better material. Examples include R22, R28, R49, and R50.

proposals.name: Stock dialogue framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of recognizable conversational templates, setup formulas, greetings, or stock sentence frames. Judge only formulaic structure; do not judge whether the frame is good or effective.
proposals.rationale: A repeated submission template can leave structural fingerprints that affect reception without constituting caption quality. Examples include R25, R40, R51, and R52.

proposals.name: Identity-role markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of explicit family, dating, occupational, religious, age, or other social-role labels. Judge only amount and specificity; do not judge whether the portrayal is good.
proposals.rationale: Author identity may shape which roles appear in the text and may also influence genuine insight, making this a mixed nuisance. Examples include R14, R22, R49, and R51.

proposals.name: Sensitive-content salience
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of references to sex, exposed bodies, injury, illness, death, or other socially sensitive material. Judge only explicitness; do not judge whether it is good, appropriate, or funny.
proposals.rationale: Venue-specific sensitivity can affect reception independently of textual quality. Examples include R14, R26, R32, and R47.

proposals.name: Consumer-marketing register
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of retail, restaurant, pricing, product, promotional, or hospitality vocabulary. Judge only visible register; do not judge whether the scenario is good or relatable.
proposals.rationale: Audience targeting or commercial context can shape vocabulary and reception, while sometimes also improving audience fit. Examples include R02, R17, R34, R50, and R52.

proposals.name: Quantification density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of explicit numerals, counts, weights, durations, distances, or other measurements. Judge only quantity and salience; do not judge whether specificity is good.
proposals.rationale: Numbers and measurements are conspicuous textual cues that may predict reception without being intrinsic evidence of quality. Examples include R14, R19, R24, R38, and R44.
